Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Wednesday, 31 July 2024 at 10.00am
(Day 041)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Daniel Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Hilbert Chiu with Ms Emily Aitken for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Good morning.
MR FULLER: Good morning, Commissioner. I call Daniel
Angelico of the College of Intensive Care Medicine of
Australia and New Zealand.
<DANIEL ANGELICO, sworn: [10.02am]
<EXAMINATION BY MR FULLER:
MR FULLER: Q. Mr Angelico, my name is Dan Fuller, I'm
one of the counsel assisting the Commissioner and I'll be
asking you some questions this morning.
A. Sure.
Q. Firstly, you provided a witness statement to assist
the Commission, which is dated 12 July 2024. Do you have
a copy of that with you?
A. I do.
Q. Have you had the opportunity to read that recently?
A. I have.
Q. And is everything in that statement true and correct
to the best of your knowledge and belief?
A. Correct.
MR FULLER: Commissioner, that will be tendered in due
course, but it is proposed to be exhibit H6.3.
THE COMMISSIONER: Yes, thank you.
MR FULLER: Q. Mr Angelico, you are the chief executive
officer of the college; is that right?
A. That is correct.
Q. How long have you held that role for?
A. In a permanent capacity for two years, previously
a year of acting from '21 to '22. But previously before
that I've been with the college for - since 2006 so I've
been there a very long time and started in the training
department, so have a good grasp on everything in that
statement.
Q. What was the role that you held before you started
acting as chief executive officer?
A. It was the general manager of training.

Q. Firstly, can you tell us what your role as chief
executive officer involves?
A. Yes. So we have a - we're a not-for-profit with
a governing board made up of intensive care specialists.
My role is to support the board in driving the college
forward in terms of our purpose, which is to train
specialist doctors in the field of intensive care. I focus
on the operational aspect. We have 49 staff that are under
my purview and we have various functions that are all
geared towards training intensive care specialists.
Q. You are not, yourself, a medical doctor; is that
right?
A. I am non-clinical; that's correct.
Q. So do we take it that the clinical expertise comes
through the college's council; is that right?
A. That is correct, and the various committees that
report in to the board are made up of specialists but also
educational experts in different fields, to drive the
curriculum and anything clinical, whilst also the board is
a - you will find the majority of the board members are
working clinicians, so this is a non-paid - anything they
give to the college is non-paid.
Q. Just having a look on page 1 of your witness
statement, in the first paragraph under item 1, you tell us
that the college is the professional body responsible for
the training, assessment and accreditation of intensive
care specialists in both Australia and New Zealand.
A. Yes.
Q. Do you see the college as having any broader role in
advocating for the interests of its fellows?
A. We do. I do think that's the case. Are you referring
to fellows in other jurisdictions or --
Q. Fellows of the college in Australia and New Zealand?
A. We do.
Q. But are we right in thinking that from the college's -
from your college's perspective, its primary role is
training, assessment and accreditation of specialists? Is
that fair?
A. It is. However, once someone goes through the
training program and becomes a fellow, we very much

consider ourselves helping them on their continual
education journey, so once you become a fellow, we don't
expect you to stop evolving and learning. CPD is a big
part of a fellow's journey, and there are different phases
of being a fellow that we consider the college is very much
a part of helping them, all the way through to eventual
retirement, when they finish their clinical work.
Q. Do you see any part of the college's role as including
advocating for trainees or fellows in the context of
workplace disputes?
A. We do, however, there is a fine line, because there is
the Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society,
which is a body that is a sister body of ours, that do
focus a lot more on advocating in that space. However,
because a lot of our doctors are the subject matter
experts, we feel like we do have a lot of value to give
when trying to solve - if we're talking about workforce -
trying to be a part of that solution, which I think it's
a multi-pronged attack. I don't thing one body can solve
workforce in Australia, New Zealand, and it's very
different in different jurisdictions. So we are part of
the solution, I feel.
Q. Leaving aside general questions of workforce - for
example, numbers and distribution - in terms of, for
example, complaints of a trainee or a fellow being bullied,
harassed, discriminated against, those sorts of complaints,
what do you see the college's role as being?
A. Yes, one of support. Like, in terms of a complaint
coming through from a trainee or a fellow that happens at
a hospital, at a particular site, we don't necessarily have
the jurisdictional power to do too much but we want to be
providers of help and support for both the trainee and the
fellow, with the local jurisdiction or the local HR
department or whatever it may be.
Some jurisdictions, it's a state-based approach to HR;
others it's a site-based approach. So our complaints
policy and our - which are, I think, available on our
website - do detail that. We don't have too much
jurisdictional power however we don't want to ignore things
that are going on in our accredited units.
Q. I'll come back to that a little bit later.
A. Sure.

Q. Just in terms of the training programs offered by the
college, are we right in understanding that the college's
training programs in intensive care medicine are the only
way for a doctor, based in Australia, to be registered as
a specialist in those fields?
A. That's a very complex question. At the moment,
there's a lot of work being done in the SIMG space with the
Kruk report, and I believe that there's an expedited
pathway for specialists to come into the country and be
registered as a specialist, however, they don't have to be
attached to a college. But, like I said, it's a very
complex question and --
Q. Sorry, to interrupt you. If we just leave aside the
question of international medical graduates, if I'm not an
international medical graduate and I want to be registered
as a specialist in intensive care medicine, I need to
complete a training program through your college; is that
right?
A. We're not the ones to give specialists recognition or
registration. We offer the fellowship. It's a different
body that provides the specialist registration, that's the
Medical Board of Australia, Ahpra. Most - so that's not
the college's remit.
Q. But if I want to be registered with the Medical Board,
through the Medical Board of Australia process in a
specialty, I need to have completed an accredited training
program; is that your understanding?
A. It is my understanding, however, there are multiple
pathways in order to do that. Not everything has to go
through the college. In terms of us awarding the
fellowship, there are a few different streams you can go
through in order to achieve fellowship.
There's the training pathway, which we have described
in the witness statement; there's also the SIMG pathway;
and then there's also a pathway called "Election to
fellowship", where you may be someone had a has a long
career in intensive care that is - this is all available on
our website - you may be given the fellowship based on your
services to intensive care. I don't think I can answer
specifically about the process of giving specialist
registration because it's outside my remit.
Q. All right. Just focusing on the training programs in
intensive care medicine that the college does offer, do you

accept that there is no competition in Australia or
New Zealand between the college and any other entity for
the delivery of those sorts of training programs?
A. I would agree with that.
Q. And do you agree that that lack of competition makes
it important for colleges such as yours to have fair,
effective and transparent processes for the governance and
administration of their training programs?
A. Absolutely.
Q. Are we right in understanding that your college
accredits intensive care units rather than individual
training posts?
A. That's correct.
Q. Are you able to explain the reason for the college
taking that approach?
A. It is historical. That has been the way it has been
since I've been at the college, and like I've put in the -
like we've put in the witness statement, some colleges may
accredit specific positions, however, we do not dictate how
a unit should staff its - how it should staff its unit in
terms of recruitment.
A unit would be made up of - you know, if I focus on
the JMO workforce, there could be multiple people in there
that aren't on a training program that are working within
a unit. There would be some that are college trainees on
their pathway to fellowship. Like I said, it's historical
that it's been that way since before I was at the college,
but, yes, you're correct, we only accredit units as opposed
to individual positions.
Q. Do you see any particular advantages of the college's
approach in accrediting units --
A. Yes.
Q. -- that is intensive care units, rather than
individual positions or posts?
A. We do. One of our focuses is to - if we focus on
New South Wales, New South Wales is made up of many
different units, different communities that have different
needs. I think it would be difficult for us to apply
something, a framework that worked in every jurisdiction
and every unit. I think you will find there are
differences between, say, a Royal North Shore and a Sydney

Children's Hospital. Each unit has different needs and,
like I said, it's very hard.
We like to work with the units in order to find out
what works best for them, especially if we're talking about
metro and rural, regional, remote, there are large
differences between each of those units. So the advantage
we see is that a unit can develop a roster that works for
them within a budget that they have and the FTE they might
have available, that the college isn't dictating how many
staff they must have.
We've got some minimum standards which are in the
documents that you have, and available on our website,
however, I think the advantage would be that different
units that have different needs can support the community
and patient care the way that they see fit in line with,
like I said, the budgets and the rostering that they need
to work within.
Q. Do the minimum standards that you just referred to
include a required ratio of supervisors to trainees?
A. Yes, there's a guide there of - and this will go back
to our comment before about the unit being made up of
a diverse group of people, and I'd like to touch on
trainees and unaccredited trainees, if I may, but usually,
we have a one to 10 ratio for our supervisors and our
trainees in order to help them through the training
program.
If you think about a supervisor of training, they
would be one of the main custodians of the training pathway
that gets delivered in the units, and so they have a large
responsibility in terms of helping people through the
pathway. The unaccredited trainees, there could be a wide
range of - a large number of those trainees in particular
units that we wouldn't have any, again, say on how someone
supervises them and what happens inside the unit with those
unaccredited trainees. But to answer your question
specifically, CICM SOTs should have about a max of 10 to
focus on, and that's in our documentation.
Q. You have described that as a guide, and I think you
said usually it would be 1 to 10. Does that mean it's not
a binding or mandatory ratio?
A. It would be - if it becomes an issue through our
accreditation process, we would work with the unit in order

to - so some units would have multiple supervisors of
training who are responsible, if the number of trainees is
beyond that 10. We'd work with the unit during
accreditation process to make sure we've got a solution
that works. But that is applied, I will say that, that is
applied, and if it's something that we find a unit isn't
adhering to, we would pop that into our accreditation
report, have that as something that we report on and we ask
the unit to report on, and we work through a solution with
them.
Q. Would we be right in thinking, then, that there's at
least some level of flexibility in the ratio depending on
the circumstances of an individual unit?
A. There would. There would, yes.
Q. And why, if at all, do you think having that
flexibility is important?
A. Sometimes it would be difficult to find supervisors of
training. I think in the witness statement we make
a distinction between, like, a CICM SOT has to go - is
provided with training and it can be a difficult job,
because of the clinical commitments they might have.
Getting protected non-clinical time and time to be
a supervisor of training is really important. We find for
the most part, a lot of our units are very supportive and
our directors are very supportive. In some units - and you
might find this in rural locations - the access to people
would be an issue. I'm not saying that is the case in
every jurisdiction or in every rural unit, however, access
to people who have enough time to focus on the SOT role
might be a challenge for some units and that's where we
would like to work with them in order to apply that
flexibility we were just talking about.
Q. So that may be a particular issue for sites in rural
and regional locations?
A. It might be.
Q. Potentially?
A. Potentially.
Q. In terms of working with the unit on those issues, are
you able to give any specific examples of things that the
college is doing or does to work with units that may have
some inherent difficulty in meeting the supervision ratio

requirements?
A. Yeah, like I said, I referenced before about the
multiple supervisor SOT hat might be worn by different
people within the unit. We've worked with units in the
past that have had trouble recruiting for staff in terms of
advertising - and I know I've been quite clear about the
college not having anything to do with recruitment. When
I say "advertising", we have a newsletter that we send out
monthly and there's a section of our website that would be
for positions vacant. We would assist in that way.
However, we have no - we don't do anything beyond that.
I do know over the journey - and this isn't specific
to New South Wales - where, yes, some units may reach out
to us if they have trouble recruiting and we would just
share it on our socials, on our e-news and on our website,
but beyond that we wouldn't be able to do anything further.
Q. Is intensive care medicine the kind of specialty where
remote or fly-in/fly-out supervision may be viable for
rural or regional locations?
A. Mmm, I can comment on that but I would like to premise
this with I do not know what it's like to live in a rural
community. However, I do understand that part of the need
in those rural settings is for people to be involved in the
community, to live there, to really feel like you're part
of a team.
Intensive care is a very team orientated specialty.
The fly-in/fly-out model I believe works, however,
sustaining relationships in terms of a - say a specialist
to trainee relationship and if there was the need for
someone to be a mentor, to help someone through the
training program, you might - and I'm not saying that this
is the case, however, it may be difficult to build
relationships and have them sustained with a fly-in/fly-out
model, however, there might be some units that to staff
their roster, that has to be the way it is.
But we find - we've done research into - and this is
not in New South Wales, but the optimal environment for
feedback and a lot of the data points to it being
a face-to-face relationship with access to people on
a daily basis.
Q. You have told us on page 3 of your statement about
three-quarters of the way down, that exposure to

cardiothoracic neurosurgical and trauma intensive care
units is required as part of the core training for
intensive care training --
A. Yes.
Q. -- have I understood that correctly?
A. You have.
Q. Is it the case that, in order to be accredited, a site
needs to offer experience in each of those areas?
A. It would - you are correct. I can clarify a little
bit. There'd be certain units that see a certain number of
cases in those sub-specialties that allow us to say if
a trainee went there, they would see - they would have
enough exposure to that sub-specialty that they could tick
off those three sub-specialties.
So you would find that a lot of the tertiary centres
have that and that's based on - I think we provided you
with some links to our accredited units on our website, and
some of the bigger tertiary units would have all of the
sub-specialties, whereas some of the rural units simply
don't have the case mix to tick that off. So it would be -
it has nothing to do with the quality of a particular unit,
it's more just the case mix that flows through that unit,
would enable them to have different sub-specialties.
Q. And if a rural unit didn't have a case mix that
included all of those sub-specialties, it wouldn't be able
to be accredited by the college; is that right?
A. No. They would still get accreditation, however, they
might not get those sub-specialties, and on our website,
you'll see that there are some units that allow a trainee
to spend a maximum of six months, then it can go up to 12,
or you could spend more time there, because they've got the
patients going through that provide them with that - those
sub-specialty exposures.
Some of the more rural units, you might find
a patient, a complex case would be flown to a different
location, because they would have the support network
there, and again, I don't want it to come across as if it's
an indictment on that particular rural unit; it's just the
case mix.
Q. If I'm a trainee in an accredited rural unit that
doesn't offer me exposure to any cases in, say,

neurosurgical --
A. Yes.
Q. -- how do I go about getting the experience I need or
the exposure I need in that area to complete my training
requirements?
A. Yes, you would have to move to a unit that provided
you with that exposure. We don't have - and I'll circle
back to the recruitment, but we - because we don't have
any - our trainee body is quite transient and they would
move around, our training program is quite flexible, and
that can have some really good pros, absolutely, but it
also has some drawbacks.
A trainee's journey to fellowship, two trainees would
be very different. They would be required to plan ahead
and know what they need to do in order to become a fellow,
and you'll find that a lot of trainees would break up their
training around our exams and around things in their life
that are going on in terms of whether it be a dual
specialty - and I've referenced that in the witness
statement, we do have a lot of trainees that are dual,
that are training with two specialties, and that circles
back to my point around intensive care being a team sport.
Intensive care is made up with people of varied
backgrounds and various skill sets, which makes intensive
care a good melting pot of skill and experience. You can't
have that without people doing multiple fellowships,
getting multiple - different experience in different areas.
The trainees that we find can get through the
program - and this is the vast majority - they would plan
ahead and, to answer your question, they would look at what
they've got left and some trainees might plan three years
in advance and might move states, might move out to rural,
to focus on the exam and then come back, so they are quite
transient in nature. But it would be on them to make sure
that they acquire a position that satisfies their training
requirements.
The college is here to - but I'll go back to the
flexibility; the college is here to make sure that our
regulations, which are quite flexible, are applied. So if
they need help in navigating that pathway, we're here to
help.

Q. How might the college help them navigate that pathway?
A. Yes, like, in terms of - we find we've got our
state-based committees, which are on our website, are made
up of clinicians in a particular jurisdiction. We've had
experience in the past, if a trainee is struggling to
complete a requirement, we find ourselves being good at
connecting people and brokering relationships, so we would
refer them to the state committee.
If someone's finding it difficult to get a position,
whether it be an anaesthetic position - and I think we've
referenced medicine and anaesthetics in our statement,
about being potential bottlenecks, and the things we're
doing around those I can touch on as well to basically try
and minimise those bottlenecks for trainees.
We find doing an exam can be a challenge for some
people, and our statistics would show that people that do
multiple attempts at the exam might find it harder to
complete the training program, but that's where - there are
some limitations in terms of the college and what we can
and can't do for trainees to get them through but we like
to think we can connect people to broker those
relationships so that if they need to find a position for
neurosurgery, they can.
Q. So in the case of your college, it's ultimately up to
the trainees' initiative to, for example, apply for and
obtain the positions they need to complete the required
components of their training; that's right?
A. That's correct.
Q. And so for your specialties, that is intensive care
medicine, there's no rotation or network system by which
a trainee can apply at the beginning and then be
effectively automatically rotated around the rotations they
need to complete their necessary training?
A. Am I allowed to focus on areas outside of New South
Wales or would you just like it specific to New South
Wales?
Q. Just starting with New South Wales, to your knowledge,
there's no such system in place in New South Wales; is that
right?
A. Nothing that's administered by the college.
Q. Is there a system that you're aware of that's

administered by someone else in New South Wales?
A. Not specifically. There are in other jurisdictions,
which I can touch on if you like.
Q. Yes, please. Can you tell us about such a system that
exists in another jurisdiction?
A. Yes. Queensland Health have a training pathway which
I think is publicly available - information on that is
publicly available - where exactly what you just said about
trainees applying to a pathway and getting - have that
shepherding through the training pathway and that advocacy
on behalf of the trainee. That does have its drawbacks,
but it does - it is a way that people who don't know how to
find a particular position, that's a support network for
them.
The college of intensive care recently received FATES
funding, government funding, to develop a program in WA,
and the idea with the federal government funding for FATES
is that they give you some money to start with and then
you've got to look for ways to make that sustainable after
their funding has run out, and we - again, we brokered that
relationship between our fellows and a local training body
in WA to start a pathway. That is really new; it's just
started. However, there are two examples of what you're
alluding to there with your question around training
pathways and support networks for trainees to get through
the program and find those jobs. I don't know how
successful WA will be yet because it's very new.
Q. Firstly, when you were describing the Queensland
system or model, you mentioned that it had some drawbacks.
Can you elaborate on those, please?
A. Yes. You might find that there'd be people that
don't - and again if we refer to - people don't just have
training going on in their lives, they might have multiple
things, work/life balance, partners that are also doctors,
we find that can also impact a trainee's ability to move to
different places. So yes, they might have an anaesthetic
rotation they need to complete and the training pathway has
provided them with options, however, they're just not
feasible for a range of reasons, and sometimes that could
be family, it could be things outside of the college that
we can't control. So the pathway is only as powerful as
the trainee's ability to undertake it, if that makes sense.
I don't see doctors being different to any other

profession in terms of work/life balance challenges and
things come up in life that take them in a different
direction.
Q. So am I right in thinking that, from the college's
perspective, to the extent there is a pathway or rotation
or network model implemented, it needs to incorporate
flexibility to allow for doctors' family life and the like?
A. Correct. And I don't know if I specifically mentioned
this, but on our website we have a parental leave policy.
The reason why I'm referencing that is because we think
that's quite a good progressive supportive thing for
parents wanting to work but also have a family. That can
sometimes be incongruent with a trainee's ability to get
through the program in a certain amount of time, so having
a flexible training program is great.
Having supportive parental leave policies is also
good. However, that might limit someone's ability - sorry,
prolong someone's ability to become a fellow in a certain
amount of time. Then you also need the units and the
jurisdiction, whether it be a director or a unit that's
also supportive of someone having work/life balance or
changing their direction halfway through a training
program.
So it's very difficult for us to say there will be X
amount of fellows in 2026, because of the flexibility we
have in our program, which we think is also a good thing
and it promotes trainees being able to focus on multiple
disciplines and they can take different pathways in their
career. However, it does have an effect on someone's
ability to get through the program.
Q. This flexibility that we've been discussing and
I think the way you put it earlier was that part of the
trainee cohort at least is somewhat transient, they move
around regularly?
A. Yes.
Q. Do you know if that's a particular issue for intensive
care medicine as a specialty compared with others?
A. I don't believe so. Like, every year we get - so
I think, again, our trainee selection policy was referenced
in the witness statement and it's on our website around how
we select trainees, and it is quite a - I don't want to say
a low bar, because that gives the impression that we don't

want to look for quality, however, we make sure that the
barrier to training with us is not insurmountable. We get
really healthy numbers; like, last year we had 222 people
across Australia and New Zealand join the pathway - join
our training pathway.
The attrition rate through training is for a number of
reasons. We do graduate, say, 70 to 80 people per year,
but, like, we get on 200 people. We don't graduate 200
people, it doesn't work like that, because everyone's
journey is slightly different and they take different
pathways to get to that end point of fellowship. So at the
moment, I do understand, and I don't think I should name
them, but there would be colleges that prescribe trainees
with particular pathways and it's quite - not rigid but
they would outline their training pathway for them. We do
not do that.
We've found in recent times that flexibility is
becoming more and more of a need for our trainees because
of work/life balance, and families and things change, and
we want to be there to support the trainee through, as
opposed to being obstructive, but it does come at a price,
I guess, in terms of flexibility has to equal a long time
to do something.
Q. If a pathway or network model could be implemented in
New South Wales, including rural and metro sites, that
gives trainees the amount of training they need in each of
the required sub-specialities but with a level of
flexibility that you've described, do you think that would
be a model worthwhile considering?
A. Yes, considering, and we would be very keen to be part
of this solution. For us, we also apply standards, and
what you will find is sometimes our applying a standard
might mean a trainee doesn't progress as expected. And
whether it be an exam or during their clinical training,
not all trainees will finish a term successfully, for
various reasons. Whether it be performance, culture,
personality differences, there are things that would - and
this is the minority, but there are things that would
change someone's direction through the training pathway.
So it's worth exploring, I definitely think the
college has a role in being part of it, and NSW Health have
been tasked with being the leaders of a health work task
force across Australia. We're very keen to be a part of

that. And I think data and understanding where trainees
are and where they want to go, that's probably the missing
piece. You could have static data that says there are
100 trainees in New South Wales in 2024, however, you don't
know what those people are thinking and what their next
move is and what they've got on their plate. So it's very
hard to say the exact number of trainees will be the same
2024, 2025 and onwards.
Q. Just on the issue of data, on page 2 of your statement
you've told us, for example, that the college is not able
to comment on the demand for services in New South Wales?
A. Yes.
Q. It doesn't have access to any data on the demand for
services. Is the absence of - is the lack of access to
data the reason why the college can't comment on demand for
services?
A. Yes, and also we would think that there'd be a number
of different bodies that could comment on the demand,
because whether it be a unit, whether it be the executive
of that unit, a local health district, there would be
multiple players in that space that would understand the
demand, the specific demand of a hospital, of a network, of
a state.
Like, I think there are different levels there and we
are just not in a position to comment on whether or not
there is a maldistribution of trainees or if there is - if
our number of trainees are meeting the demands of the unit.
Like I said, it goes back to that JMO workforce is made up
of a number of different stakeholders, not all of them are
college trainees.
Q. Would it be the college's preference to have access to
more data on workforce distribution and demand for services
in order to be able to make a contribution on those issues?
A. Yes, and I think stats are a good start in terms of
two-way communication. So, like, we would happily share
what we know about our trainees and then if information was
coming down to us as well, I think that would be helpful.
